A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TACO research work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original MVC and maximum-clique experiments, including static, distribution-shifted, and dynamic evaluations, optimization trajectories, and hyperparameter analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original MIS, ConsFormer/MaxCut, COExpander, seed-averaging, and perturbed-gradient experiments. Some comparison scores are explicitly attributed to prior work.

M1.justification: Standard TACO's shrink-and-perturb initialization and online parameter reuse remain unchanged. Appendix B.6 introduces an optional TACO-PGD combination that also injects perturbations during gradient updates, a limited procedural extension rather than a redesign.

E1.justification: v2 adds MIS on 1,000-node random regular graphs, training on degree 20 and evaluating degrees 5, 7, 10, and 20. It also adds MaxCut on GSET across graph sizes from 800 to at least 3,000 nodes. These expand task requirements and graph populations beyond the retained MVC/MC coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated COExpander configurations on Twitter/COLLAB MVC and MC, plus PGD comparisons on Twitter. The new MaxCut comparison includes ConsFormer and fine-tuning alongside reported baselines such as SDP, RUNCSP, ECO-DQN, ESCORD, ANYCSP, and OR-Tools. Original comparator sets remain present.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce substantial new protocols: MIS uses 3,000 training graphs, 50 evaluation graphs per degree, and approximation ratios normalized by theoretical upper bounds; MaxCut uses ConsFormer with 100 adaptation steps and percentage gaps to best-known cuts. COExpander comparisons add configuration sweeps and one-/three-step TACO settings. Retained MVC/MC protocols are unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond retaining the original sensitivity and seed-budget analyses, v2 adds best-versus-average seed comparisons and tests perturbations before adaptation versus during gradient updates, including their combination. Table 15 also adds a full random-initialization control. These investigate selection effects and alternative explanations for TACO's gains.

E5.justification: Appendix B.4 adds performance averaged across all eight input seeds alongside best-seed performance, changing the reported statistical aggregation. Existing seed counts and plus/minus reporting remain; neither additional independent training runs nor new confidence intervals or significance tests are established.

E6.justification: Original table values are retained, while v2 adds substantial results for COExpander, MaxCut, MIS, seed averages, and PGD. For example, Table 7 reports an 800-node MaxCut gap of 0.80% for TACO versus 0.98% for fine-tuning and 0.91% for reproduced ConsFormer; published ConsFormer is better at 0.31%. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 scores.

T1.justification: Appendix B.5 adds an explicit MIS loss definition: a negative node-selection sum plus an edge-conflict penalty. This is a limited formal addition adopted from prior work. Existing CO, MVC, and MC formulations remain, and no new theorem, proof, or convergence guarantee is provided.

C1.justification: The central claims remain that naive fine-tuning can underperform random initialization and that model-agnostic TACO bridges generalizable and instance-specific optimization with negligible additional overhead. The expanded task and backbone lists broaden supporting evidence without materially redefining these already broad claims.

C2.justification: v2 reframes the mechanism from potentially escaping poor local minima toward favorable initialization and faster attainment of better optima. It adds interpretations of compute scaling versus COExpander and the MIS RRG-10 exception, suggesting more updates could close that gap. The existing limitations paragraph is unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, clarifies that model-specific random initialization can supply perturbations, and documents MIS generation, loss, learning rate, and SP settings. It also gives ConsFormer adaptation budgets and timings. Existing hardware and MVC/MC implementation details remain unchanged.

R1.justification: New references and discussion connect the experiments to COExpander, ConsFormer, perturbed gradient descent, MIS bounds, and additional MaxCut methods. Positioning relative to shrink-and-perturb, Meta-EGN, and test-time adaptation remains essentially unchanged. Publication-metadata updates do not constitute new related work.

P1.justification: The introduction and method exposition are condensed, the motivating failure-mode discussion moves into renamed Section 2.3, and Appendix B gains descriptive subsections. Publication information and acknowledgments are added. Most prose and the overall section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with COExpander and MaxCut comparison tables, MIS trajectory figures and results, and seed-average and PGD tables. Existing figures and tables are retained, with relocation and renumbering; the sensitivity table gains a control row and expanded caption.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the model-agnostic claim, previously supported only by closely related EGN backbones, through ConsFormer/MaxCut and additional MIS experiments. COExpander comparisons and seed/perturbation controls also address important evidential gaps. Some new wording overstates uniform superiority over COExpander, and MaxCut gains concern the weaker reproduced ConsFormer baseline rather than its published scores. These qualifications limit the conclusions but leave a substantial overall improvement in empirical support.
